title: IoT · 05 · LPWAN, application protocols and WSN routing
notes: PDF page numbers are used. The bank covers LPWAN, LoRaWAN, Sigfox, publish/subscribe, MQTT, CoAP and every named routing family in the deck.

LPWAN operating limits and Sigfox message budgets are lecture scenarios, not current service-plan or regulatory guarantees. LoRa denotes the radio modulation/PHY; LoRaWAN adds MAC and network organization. Gateways need not translate every protocol layer in every deployment.

MQTT correction beyond the slides: its fixed header has one control byte plus a Remaining Length field of 1–4 bytes, not a universal fixed 24-bit header. Retained delivery stores the retained value per topic, not an unlimited history. QoS is scoped to a protocol delivery leg, not arbitrary exactly-once application side effects. Source: https://docs.oasis-open.org/mqtt/mqtt/v3.1.1/os/mqtt-v3.1.1-os.html sections 2.2, 3.3 and 4.3.

CoAP corrections beyond the slides: tokens correlate requests and responses, while Message IDs match ACK/RST and support duplicate detection. A separate response uses a new Message ID but retains the request token. An empty ACK is not the application response. RFC 7252 default MAX_RETRANSMIT is 4, not three. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7252.html sections 4.2, 4.4, 4.8 and 5.2–5.3.

Architecture comparisons depend on topology, traffic and polling interval; REST versus pub/sub alone does not determine hop count, latency, energy or packet loss. All rate/delay examples explicitly state idealizing assumptions.

PEGASIS parallel aggregation is the particular staged model shown on pages 132–135; logarithmic delay requires compatible simultaneous transmissions. Multihop and aggregation do not guarantee lower energy or latency under all conditions.

questions.prompt: Describe the device, channel, gateway and application roles in an IoT system. Why should gateway conversion be described per protocol layer rather than as one universal operation?
questions.answer: Sensors measure, controllers decide and actuators act; channels carry communication. A gateway connects access devices to the wider network and applications. It may bridge, route or proxy depending on the protocols, so conversion responsibilities depend on the actual stack.
questions.explanation: A gateway is an architectural role, not a guarantee that every packet is translated at every layer.

questions.prompt: A remote meter sends a few bytes hourly over several kilometers; a nearby network streams rich sensor data. Compare the suitability of LPWAN and WPAN and state the central trade-offs.
questions.answer: LPWAN suits infrequent small long-range reports with low average energy use; WPAN is suited to shorter-range communication with higher local capacity and optional relaying. Range, data volume, duty cycle and latency requirements drive the choice.
questions.explanation: Wide coverage does not make a technology suitable for high-rate or low-latency traffic.

questions.prompt: Why is a long-battery-life LPWAN sensor not automatically suitable for a control loop requiring 1 ms response and very high reliability?
questions.answer: LPWAN usually trades data rate and downlink availability for energy and range. Sleeping devices, slow serialization, contention and limited receive opportunities can prevent bounded millisecond responses.
questions.explanation: Average energy efficiency and dependable real-time behavior are different requirements.
key_points: Low rate or sleep causes delay

questions.prompt: Distinguish LoRa from LoRaWAN. Explain the basic end-device–gateway–server path and where IP can enter that path.
questions.answer: LoRa supplies chirp-spread-spectrum radio communication; LoRaWAN defines MAC behavior and network organization. End devices send to one or more gateways, which forward over an IP backhaul to a server that processes and deduplicates received traffic.
questions.explanation: The constrained access link need not carry an ordinary IP stack for gateways to use IP upstream.

questions.prompt: Why can reducing the effective radio data rate extend useful range while hurting capacity and latency? Explain the role of airtime rather than just bits per packet.
questions.answer: More robust low-rate settings can make weak signals decodable, but the same payload then occupies the channel longer. Greater airtime delays completion, spends active energy and leaves fewer opportunities for other traffic.
questions.explanation: Range improvement comes with shared-medium costs, rather than free extra coverage.

questions.prompt: Why does LoRaWAN avoid forwarding through neighboring battery sensors? How can reception by multiple gateways improve robustness without requiring every copy to reach the application?
questions.answer: Direct access avoids battery-powered relays carrying others' traffic. Multiple gateways may hear the same uplink, offering reception diversity. The network server removes redundant copies before normal application delivery.
questions.explanation: Redundancy at reception and duplicate application events are different issues.

questions.prompt: Compare Class A, B and C downlink opportunities. Which class best fits a rarely reporting battery meter and which best fits a powered actuator needing prompt commands?
questions.answer: A listens in two windows after its own uplink and minimizes energy use; B adds scheduled beacon-synchronized receive slots; C listens nearly continuously except while transmitting. A suits the meter; C suits the powered actuator.
questions.explanation: Class B provides an intermediate scheduling/energy trade-off.
key_points: B scheduled and C near-continuous listening
Correct application choices and energy trade-off

questions.prompt: A command becomes ready just after a Class A device's receive windows close. Why is transmission time alone insufficient to predict delivery delay? Compare Class C.
questions.answer: Class A normally must wait for a later uplink and its receive opportunity before the downlink can be delivered. That availability wait may dominate serialization. Class C offers near-continuous reception, reducing that waiting component at higher energy cost.
questions.explanation: The deck's simple latency exercise must not be generalized without receive-window timing.
key_points: Wait for next valid Class A opportunity
Class C lower waiting but higher energy

questions.prompt: For a 13-byte payload serialized at 1 kbit/s over a 10 km radio path, compute serialization and propagation time with c=3*10^8 m/s. Ignore headers. Which term dominates, and what omitted delay can still be larger?
questions.answer: Serialization is 104 ms; propagation is about 33.3 us. Serialization dominates these two terms, while receive-window scheduling or waiting for access can add substantially more.
questions.explanation: Distance-induced delay is not necessarily the main delay in a slow IoT link.

questions.prompt: Compare the deck's Sigfox uplink mechanism with a conventional acknowledged transmission. Why send copies at different times and frequencies, and what does that fail to guarantee?
questions.answer: The lecture describes unacknowledged copies on different frequencies and times to gain diversity against fading, collisions and interference. The sender still lacks explicit delivery confirmation, and all copies may fail.
questions.explanation: Redundancy improves reception probability without becoming an acknowledgement protocol.
key_points: No explicit ACK in described uplink

questions.prompt: Using only the lecture scenario of 140 uplinks/day with 12 payload bytes each, calculate the average useful uplink rate. Why is it different from the instantaneous radio bitrate?
questions.answer: The daily payload is 140*12*8=13440 bits; divided by 86400 s this is about 0.156 bit/s. It averages long idle periods and message-budget limits, while radio bitrate describes bits during an active transmission.
questions.explanation: This is a scenario calculation, not a claim about current service offerings.
key_points: Average reporting rate differs from active PHY rate

questions.prompt: How do device ID, authentication/error-check fields, gateways and the backend contribute to the Sigfox path described in the slides? Why may the backend need duplicate removal?
questions.answer: Device IDs identify report origins; authentication and frame checks support authenticity and error detection. Gateways forward radio traffic to the IP backend, which stores/exposes data to applications. Multiple gateways or repeated transmissions can deliver copies requiring deduplication.
questions.explanation: Identification, integrity checks and forwarding are different responsibilities.
key_points: Backend receives through gateways and removes copies

questions.prompt: Compare polling request/response with publish/subscribe for a sensor that changes rarely. Explain topic subscription and one benefit and one risk of introducing a broker.
questions.answer: Polling repeatedly asks for current data; pub/sub delivers events when published to subscribed topics. A broker matches/distributes events, reducing needless polling, but can become a bottleneck or failure point.
questions.explanation: Publisher and consumer need not know one another's network identities to exchange topic-based data.

questions.prompt: Explain the roles of publish, subscribe and unsubscribe, and why distributed brokers do not automatically remove every bottleneck.
questions.answer: Publishing submits an event; subscribing expresses interest; unsubscribing removes it. Multiple cooperating brokers can spread load and add redundancy, but their queues, links and coordination can still constrain throughput or availability.
questions.explanation: Changing a subscription changes event delivery, not the sensor's underlying measurements.

questions.prompt: A broker receives 120 events/s but can forward only 100 events/s, with a queue initially empty and room for 1000 events. In a constant-rate lossless-in-service model, when does it fill? Name two possible remedies.
questions.answer: Backlog grows at 20 events/s, filling in 50 s. Reduce incoming traffic through filtering/aggregation or rate control, or increase service capacity through faster processing or distribution.
questions.explanation: A larger buffer alone postpones loss but does not correct a persistent arrival/service imbalance.

questions.prompt: A slide compares REST and pub/sub latency using particular paths. Why is it unsafe to conclude that pub/sub is always slower? What determines event-to-application delay?
questions.answer: The result depends on link rates, hop count, broker processing/queues and polling interval. Pub/sub adds broker forwarding but can avoid waiting for the next poll; REST can have a short path yet long event-detection delay.
questions.explanation: An architectural label does not fix the timing of every deployment.

questions.prompt: A 200-byte report crosses three store-and-forward links at 100 kbit/s, 1 Gbit/s and 1 Gbit/s. Ignore all other delays and headers. Compare latency when all three links are 100 kbit/s.
questions.answer: Sum the serialization times: 1600/100000+2*1600/10^9=16.0032 ms. With three 100 kbit/s links, total latency is 48 ms.
questions.explanation: For one complete packet, each store-and-forward hop adds serialization even if pipeline throughput can be higher.

questions.prompt: An event waits 500 ms for polling. A 100-byte request and 200-byte response each cross three 100 kbit/s store-and-forward links. Ignoring other costs, calculate time from event to received response.
questions.answer: The request takes 3*800/100000=24 ms; response takes 3*1600/100000=48 ms. Including polling wait gives 500+24+48=572 ms.
questions.explanation: The event's waiting time is part of application freshness even before the first request is transmitted.

questions.prompt: Describe MQTT's relationship to TCP and the broker. What do CONNECT/CONNACK and PINGREQ/PINGRESP add beyond a TCP connection?
questions.answer: MQTT is an application pub/sub protocol carried over TCP. CONNECT/CONNACK establishes MQTT-level session acceptance; keepalive ping exchanges detect an idle connection that is no longer usable. TCP byte delivery alone does not describe MQTT session state.
questions.explanation: Transport reliability and application-protocol session behavior operate at different layers.

questions.prompt: Compare QoS 0, 1 and 2 in terms of loss, duplicates and protocol cost. For QoS 2, what must you avoid claiming about arbitrary application side effects?
questions.answer: QoS 0 offers at-most-once delivery; QoS 1 can redeliver; QoS 2 suppresses duplicates for its MQTT delivery exchange with extra state/messages. It does not by itself guarantee exactly-once effects across arbitrary application code or independent delivery legs.
questions.explanation: Reliability semantics must be interpreted at the layer and scope where they are defined.
key_points: 0 at most once and 1 at least once

questions.prompt: Write the MQTT message sequence for QoS 1 and QoS 2. Why is tracking exchange state and packet identifiers necessary when replies may be lost?
questions.answer: QoS 1 uses PUBLISH–PUBACK. QoS 2 uses PUBLISH–PUBREC–PUBREL–PUBCOMP. Identifiers and retained exchange state let peers associate retries/replies with an existing delivery rather than processing every arrival as a new publication.
questions.explanation: More messages alone do not provide duplicate suppression without state.
key_points: Track retries and completion with identifiers/state

questions.prompt: Name the parts of an MQTT control packet. Correct the claim that every fixed header is exactly 24 bits, and explain the purpose of RETAIN on a PUBLISH.
questions.answer: Packets have a fixed header and, depending on type, a variable header and payload. The fixed header has a control byte plus 1–4 Remaining Length bytes. RETAIN stores a topic's retained value for later subscribers.
questions.explanation: Standards clarification: https://docs.oasis-open.org/mqtt/mqtt/v3.1.1/os/mqtt-v3.1.1-os.html sections 2.2 and 3.3.1.3. Retained values are not a full event history.

questions.prompt: Why might a constrained sensor network use MQTT-SN and a gateway instead of requiring every sensor to open a normal MQTT/TCP connection?
questions.answer: MQTT-SN adapts pub/sub communication for sensor-network constraints and can use transports such as UDP without a TCP connection from every sensor. A gateway translates the sensor-side exchanges into MQTT communication with a broker.
questions.explanation: The gateway preserves the pub/sub interaction while adapting its transport and message representation.
key_points: Gateway connects sensor protocol to MQTT broker

questions.prompt: At 250 kbit/s, suppose each MQTT control packet is artificially 200 bytes and a sender completes one exchange before starting the next. Ignoring all other delay, calculate message rates for 1-, 2- and 4-packet exchanges. Why are these only model estimates?
questions.answer: One packet takes 6.4 ms. Rates are 156.25, 78.125 and 39.0625 completed exchanges/s. Actual control sizes differ and transport headers, fragmentation, RTT, queues and pipelining change the result.
questions.explanation: The exercise isolates handshake serialization, not real MQTT-over-802.15.4 performance.
key_points: Artificial sizes and omitted timing effects

questions.prompt: How can MQTT support request/response while remaining a publish/subscribe protocol? Explain the roles of a server topic and response topic.
questions.answer: A requester subscribes for responses and publishes a request to the server's topic, including a response-topic indication. The server receives via subscription and publishes its reply to that topic through the broker.
questions.explanation: Application-level request/response is implemented using two topic-routed publication directions.
key_points: Both messages still travel via broker

questions.prompt: Why was base CoAP designed over UDP with compact binary messages? How can an HTTP/CoAP proxy connect a web application to a constrained sensor?
questions.answer: UDP and compact encoding reduce connection/message overhead for constrained devices. A proxy maps resources, methods and responses between HTTP and CoAP, such as HTTP GET to CoAP GET and a successful readout back to HTTP.
questions.explanation: UDP itself does not provide reliable delivery; the CoAP message layer can add acknowledgements and retries.
key_points: CoAP can supply reliability above UDP

questions.prompt: Distinguish CON, NON, ACK and RST in base CoAP. Is an empty ACK evidence that the requested application result is already available?
questions.answer: CON requests message acknowledgement; NON omits that exchange; ACK confirms a CON; RST rejects a message lacking suitable context. An empty ACK confirms receipt but contains no application result.
questions.explanation: Message delivery and application response are separate concerns.
key_points: Empty ACK does not provide application result

questions.prompt: What different jobs do Message ID and Token perform in CoAP? Why must they not both be described as a session identifier?
questions.answer: Message ID supports duplicate detection and ACK/RST matching. Token correlates a response with its request. They operate at different layers of the exchange, rather than representing one shared session identifier.
questions.explanation: Correction to the slides; RFC 7252 sections 4.4 and 5.3: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7252.html
key_points: Message ID for ACK/RST and duplicates
Different purposes, not one session ID

questions.prompt: A CON GET has Message ID m and Token t. Compare an immediate piggybacked response with a delayed separate CON response. Which identifiers are reused?
questions.answer: An immediate response can be carried in ACK m with Token t. For delayed processing the server sends empty ACK m, then CON with a fresh Message ID n and Token t; the client replies with ACK n.
questions.explanation: Correction to page 73: the separate response gets its own Message ID. RFC 7252 section 5.2: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7252.html
key_points: Delayed response keeps token but uses fresh ID
Client acknowledges separate CON by its ID

questions.prompt: How does a confirmable CoAP message recover from a missing ACK, and why increase timeouts between retries? Should its retry count be inferred from the slide example as a universal protocol rule?
questions.answer: The sender retransmits subject to a bounded retry policy, increasing timeout to avoid persistent aggressive traffic during loss or congestion. The slide's number is not universal; RFC 7252 defaults to four retransmissions.
questions.explanation: RFC 7252 sections 4.2 and 4.8 correct the slide example: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7252.html
key_points: Default four retransmissions, not universal slide count

questions.prompt: Choose CON or NON for (a) a replaceable temperature sample sent each second and (b) an important command. Explain why an ACK alone is insufficient to prove the intended physical action occurred.
questions.answer: NON can suit replaceable samples when occasional loss is acceptable; CON is preferable for acknowledged delivery of important commands. Even then an ACK concerns message reception; application status or a response is needed to establish command processing and physical outcome.
questions.explanation: Transporting a command and verifying an actuator's real-world state are separate steps.
key_points: NON when occasional sample loss acceptable

questions.prompt: Describe the fixed CoAP header's purpose and the roles of Token, Options and Payload. Interpret the distinction between a success response and a client-error response.
questions.answer: The base header carries version, message type, token length, code and Message ID. Token correlates responses; Options carry metadata such as resource selection; Payload carries content. Class 2 indicates success and class 4 indicates a client error.
questions.explanation: Binary encoding keeps common fields compact while options extend message meaning.

questions.prompt: For one slow sensor link at 250 kbit/s, a GET has 20 CoAP bytes and its response has 10. Each adds 8 UDP, 10 adaptation and 10 MAC bytes. Ignore other delays and fast-link serialization. Calculate round-trip serialization.
questions.answer: Request size is 48 bytes and response size 38 bytes. Total is 86*8/250000=0.002752 s, or 2.752 ms. A precise end-to-end result would also include the other links and any processing, waiting or retransmission.
questions.explanation: Headers must be counted on each direction at the layer where they are transmitted.

questions.prompt: Distinguish flat/hierarchical organization from address/data/location-based routing. Why are these classifications not mutually exclusive alternatives?
questions.answer: Flat versus hierarchical describes whether nodes have similar roles or form clusters with heads. Address-, data- and location-based schemes describe what identifies the desired destination/information. A hierarchy can forward by location or requested data.
questions.explanation: Topology/roles and forwarding criteria describe different dimensions of a routing design.

questions.prompt: Explain how traffic aggregation can save transmissions yet create an energy bottleneck at a cluster head. Name one mitigation and one latency cost.
questions.answer: Combining readings removes redundancy or reduces packet counts, but the head must receive, process and forward others' traffic. Rotate heads or distribute the load; buffering and processing before forwarding can add latency.
questions.explanation: Network-wide savings do not imply equal energy savings at every device.

questions.prompt: Compare proactive, reactive and hybrid routing for a mostly idle sensor network and for frequent latency-sensitive traffic.
questions.answer: Proactive routing maintains paths with recurring control traffic, reducing discovery wait for frequent traffic. Reactive routing discovers on demand, saving quiet-period overhead but adding initial delay. Hybrid approaches maintain some routes proactively and discover others as needed.
questions.explanation: Energy and reaction-time trade-offs depend on traffic and topology changes.
key_points: Reactive low idle overhead with discovery delay

questions.prompt: Why can flooding deliver quickly along a short path while still being inefficient? Explain TTL and distinguish traffic implosion from overlapping sensor information.
questions.answer: Parallel copies can reach the destination via a short path, but consume energy and airtime. TTL bounds forwarding lifetime. Implosion duplicates the same datagram through different paths; overlap is redundant information generated by different sources.
questions.explanation: Bounding hop count limits persistence but does not remove all duplicate or redundant traffic.
key_points: Same packet duplicates versus overlapping content

questions.prompt: Compare forwarding one datagram by flooding with forwarding it by gossiping to one randomly chosen neighbor. Why can gossiping use fewer transmissions locally but take longer end to end?
questions.answer: Flooding sends copies toward many neighbors; gossiping chooses one. Each gossip step costs fewer transmissions but may follow detours or revisit nodes, increasing path length and delivery time.
questions.explanation: A locally cheap forwarding choice is not necessarily a shortest end-to-end route.
key_points: Many neighbors versus one random neighbor

questions.prompt: In a five-node ring with equal destination probability over the other four nodes, flooding reaches two nodes in one hop and two in two hops. Frames are 200 bytes at 250 kbit/s. Ignoring collisions and other delays, find mean first-arrival latency.
questions.answer: One-hop serialization is 1600/250000=6.4 ms. Mean distance is (1+1+2+2)/4=1.5 hops, so mean first-arrival latency is 9.6 ms.
questions.explanation: The calculation uses shortest first arrivals under ideal parallel flooding, not the total airtime spent on all copies.

questions.prompt: Trace ADV–REQ–DATA in SPIN and explain how metadata helps reduce redundant data transmissions.
questions.answer: A node advertises descriptive metadata with ADV. An interested neighbor sends REQ; the advertiser then sends DATA. Neighbors can request only information they need instead of receiving every full datagram blindly.
questions.explanation: Metadata is useful when its negotiation cost is smaller than the unnecessary data transfers avoided.
key_points: DATA follows request and avoids blind data flooding

questions.prompt: Why should a SPIN node estimate the energy needed for the whole negotiation before advertising or requesting data? What connectivity trade-off follows from withdrawing when low on energy?
questions.answer: Advertising commits to receiving a request and sending data; requesting commits to receiving data. Checking those costs prevents starting exchanges the node cannot afford, but a withdrawing intermediary may block dissemination through that route.
questions.explanation: Preserving one node's energy can reduce reachability for others.

questions.prompt: How does SPIN-BC exploit a shared broadcast channel to suppress duplicate requests? Why might a lower-energy node wait longer before requesting?
questions.answer: Interested nodes delay REQ and listen for another node's request. One request can trigger a broadcast DATA received by all interested neighbors, letting others suppress their own REQs. A lower-energy node can defer and benefit from a better-powered requester.
questions.explanation: Broadcast overhearing is used as a useful shared result rather than repeated point-to-point work.
key_points: One DATA broadcast serves multiple listeners

questions.prompt: What do retransmitted requests/data recovery and periodic advertisements add in SPIN-RL? Why does this not guarantee delivery through an uninterested or unavailable forwarding bottleneck?
questions.answer: They offer recovery opportunities when a requested DATA message is lost or an advertisement was missed. However, data still needs a viable chain of participating nodes; loss recovery cannot create interest or physical connectivity at a bottleneck.
questions.explanation: Protocol reliability features are conditional on an available forwarding path.

questions.prompt: Trace an interest from a sink to sensors in Directed Diffusion. What is a gradient, which way does it point, and how is returning data forwarded?
questions.answer: The sink disseminates an attribute-based interest. Each receiver records interest state and gradients toward neighbors from which interest arrived, including requested rate/lifetime. Matching sensor data follows those gradients back toward interested receivers.
questions.explanation: Interest propagation establishes reverse-direction information for subsequent data delivery.
key_points: Matching data follows gradients toward sink

questions.prompt: Directed Diffusion has several gradients for the same interest. What does reinforcement accomplish, and why do timestamps and expiry matter?
questions.answer: Reinforcement favors a useful path, for example by requesting a higher data rate along a lower-latency route. Timestamps and lifetimes age out obsolete interest/gradient state so forwarding adapts instead of persisting forever.
questions.explanation: Multipath discovery and selective sustained delivery can serve different stages of communication.

questions.prompt: Compare SPIN's data-driven negotiation with Directed Diffusion's interest-driven delivery. Who initiates dissemination, and how is unnecessary data forwarding reduced?
questions.answer: SPIN begins with a producer advertising available data, followed by requests. Directed Diffusion begins with a sink disseminating interests that establish gradients. Both avoid blindly forwarding all data by matching offered information to demand.
questions.explanation: The two are data-centric but differ in how demand is learned and forwarding state is established.

questions.prompt: Describe LEACH's setup and steady-state phases. How do cluster-head rotation, aggregation and TDMA each contribute to energy efficiency?
questions.answer: Setup elects heads, forms clusters and distributes schedules. Steady state collects data in TDMA slots and aggregates it at heads for the sink. Rotation spreads head workload; aggregation reduces redundancy; scheduled access limits intra-cluster contention and unnecessary listening.
questions.explanation: The selected heads incur extra work, so a permanent choice can exhaust a few critical nodes.
key_points: Aggregation and TDMA reduce communication waste

questions.prompt: For eligible nodes, T=P/(1-P*(r mod (1/P))); ineligible nodes have T=0. With P=0.2, calculate T at r=0 and r=4 within an epoch. What is the purpose of eligibility G?
questions.answer: At r=0, T=0.2; at r=4, T=0.2/(1-0.8)=1. G excludes nodes already selected in the current five-round epoch, preventing repeated head selection while giving remaining eligible nodes a rising chance.
questions.explanation: The threshold applies only to eligible nodes; a high threshold does not override exclusion.
key_points: Eligibility prevents repeat selection within epoch

questions.prompt: In a five-node LEACH epoch, four nodes have already been cluster heads and the remaining node has 4% battery. Why may baseline LEACH still select it, and what does XLEACH try to improve?
questions.answer: Baseline eligibility/threshold selection does not account for remaining energy, so the only eligible node can become head. XLEACH adjusts selection using energy and time since selection to reduce assigning demanding head work to weak batteries.
questions.explanation: Equal historical role rotation is not the same as equal remaining energy capacity.
key_points: Energy-aware threshold aims to improve assignment

questions.prompt: Compare LEACH's clusters with PEGASIS's chain and rotating leader. Why can nearest-neighbor exchanges reduce transmission energy, and what topology dependency do they introduce?
questions.answer: LEACH collects within multiple clusters; PEGASIS builds a chain of neighboring nodes and rotates the node forwarding aggregated data to the sink. Short neighbor links can reduce transmit power, but chain construction and breaks affect routes and collection delay.
questions.explanation: Saving power per link does not remove coordination or topology-management costs.
key_points: Short links save power but create chain dependencies

questions.prompt: The deck's parallel aggregation example halves the active participant set each stage. For eight nodes, how many collection stages are needed? Compare an interference-constrained sequential chain and state the assumption behind the difference.
questions.answer: The parallel staged model needs log2(8)=3 collection stages; sequential collection can require 8-1=7. The shorter schedule assumes the paired transmissions can occur simultaneously without destructive interference and with the required links available.
questions.explanation: These are collection stages, excluding the final leader-to-sink transmission.
key_points: Parallelism/link feasibility assumption and final hop excluded
